Series::selu¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::selu() const
Series& Series::selu_() const

Fixed Scaled Exponential Activation¶

selu() applies a scaled exponential linear unit with fixed constants:

$$ \operatorname{selu}(x)=\lambda \begin{cases} x, & x>0,\ \alpha(e^x-1), & x\le 0, \end{cases} $$

where alpha is approximately 1.6732632423543772 and lambda is approximately 1.0507009873554805. The fixed pair is the operation’s contract; use elu() when those coefficients need to be controlled directly.

The positive branch is linear with slope greater than one. The negative branch saturates toward -lambda * alpha, approximately -1.7581, instead of decreasing without bound. This asymmetric shape is intended for networks whose initialization and architecture are designed around self-normalizing behavior; the activation alone does not guarantee that property for an arbitrary model.

Contract¶

  • Evaluation is elementwise and preserves shape, rank, and platform.

  • Floating dtype is preserved; integer and Boolean input is promoted to float32.

  • Complex input is rejected.

  • The method is out of place and leaves the receiver unchanged.

  • Reverse mode uses slope lambda on positive lanes and lambda * alpha * exp(x) on non-positive lanes. At exactly zero, the non-positive branch is used, giving slope lambda * alpha.

In-Place Form¶

selu_() is the in-place sibling of selu(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — selu_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, 0.0, 2.0});
x.selu_();
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.5201665, 0, 2.101402]

Examples¶

1. Compare the exponential and linear regions¶

const auto x = pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 3.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.selu());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.6706, -1.1113, 0.0000, 1.0507, 3.1521]

The negative values bend toward the finite lower asymptote. Positive values are scaled by the fixed factor lambda.

2. Shape is preserved for matrices¶

const auto x = pluss::make_series({{-2.0, 0.0}, {1.0, 3.0}});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.selu());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ -1.5202 0.0000 ⎤
⎣  1.0507 3.1521 ⎦

3. Integer lanes are promoted before activation¶

pluss::series::print(std::cout,
                     pluss::make_series({-2, 0, 2}).selu());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.5202, 0.0000, 2.1014]

The result is float32; neither the exponential branch nor the fixed scale is truncated to an integer.

4. Reverse mode distinguishes the zero boundary¶

auto x = pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 1.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.selu().sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.6468, 1.7581, 1.0507]

At zero the derivative comes from the exponential branch and is approximately 1.7581; immediately on the positive side it is approximately 1.0507.

5. Complex input is outside the contract¶

try {
  using Complex = std::complex<double>;
  (void)pluss::make_series(
      std::vector<Complex>{{1.0, 1.0}}, {1}).selu();
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
  std::cout << error.what() << '\n';
}

Output¶

selu: complex input is not supported

Performance¶

The operation is linear in numel(). Positive lanes require only scaling; negative lanes require an exponential. The analytic activation node keeps the forward tape compact and supports reverse and higher-order differentiation.

See Also¶

  • elu() exposes the related coefficients.

  • mish() is smooth across zero and does not saturate to the same negative constant.

  • leaky_relu() uses a linear negative branch.
